Note to readers: This tip isn't just frugal, it's physiological. Same reason coffee/tea are great in dry heat but bad in humidity or cold (they heat up your internal system and make you produce more sweat and acclimate to a higher temperature) and cold drinks are good in cold. Sleep is best in a cold environment.

Going between hot buildings and cold weather (or vice versa in summer) fucks with your body's temperature regulation and makes you more prone to disease, while also making the temperature shifts more jarring for your body. Learn layering like anyone in a cold climate throughout history did, with proper clothing you shouldn't need more than 3 layers in most weather (base, mid, shell). Also, vests and hats are awesome (insulate your core and your extremities warm themselves, gloves are rarely necessary unless you'll be out in the cold for a long time; the "90% of your heat is lost through the head" thing is a myth, but your scalp is a bunch of surface area with capillaries so it's still good to insulate it).

Polo shirts are a workplace staple for this reason. They're a great mid-range option that can work up until the early 80s (assuming med-low humidity), the only thing they lack is moisture wicking.

Basically, learn the physics behind it all and you can make informed decisions. Two related things that will save you in your situation (hot workplace, cold outside, I assume) are: Breathability of fabric (essentially how loosely it's been weaved, if you hold it up in front of a light and can't see any light, it won't breathe well, decent light transfer means that air will go through too) and how "dimpled" it is. Hard to explain this in words, but look up seersucker cloth and you'll get what I mean. Basically, air pockets for movement of air instead of trapping it under your layers.

This is actually why wool has for centuries been a staple for cold climates. It's breathable and it insulates well and it retains its warmth even while very damp (~33% saturation is the tipping point). So if you sweat because you're working outside, wool will let that sweat evaporate instead of stay trapped, and the sweat won't make you freeze once it starts getting in the fabric, and you stay warm the whole time.

Now that the last paragraph has explained to you why everybody with any hiking/survival/military experience tells you to make sure you have plenty of good wool socks, I'm going to tell you they'll save your ass. Feet are a major point where you lose temperature (part of why wearing socks to bed can make such a massive difference in how much bedding you need). Good wool socks will save your bacon if you're going between hot/cold, because you won't have sweaty feet from subpar non-breathable cotton (cotton = worst organic fiber, fuck cotton) and they'll let you get some air while inside so your feet don't fry. Shoes are also an important consideration here obviously: Arch/ankle support, insulation and structural stability (I have some cozy/comfy oxfords and street boots, but obviously if I'm doing Man Work I throw on my Red Wings). Depends a lot on your line of work, but depending on the circumstance it can totally be worth it to keep an extra pair of shoes at work to change into.

Three things I'll never compromise on (within my means): 1. Bedding 2. Clothing 3. Seating

2 & 3 can swap places depending on if my job is mostly standing or sitting, but the point is: You spend 6-10 hours of your day asleep, you spend (conservatively) 10-14 hours wearing most of your clothing and you can easily spend anywhere from 3-10 hours of your day sitting (depending on if it's part of your job or not + your hobbies).

One thing I will never regret is spending a bit of time here and there browsing craigslist for used ergonomic chairs. Do your research, but I got two steelcase LEAP (around $1k new) chairs for $150ea. Replacement parts are easy to buy online, they're built to last, and usually you can find a bunch in good condition from a small business that bought a lot when they started up and overstepped, they just go quick. Obviously this depends on lifestyle, but in my case at the time I felt it was worth getting one for work and one for home at that price.

My bed (Full, not queen/king) was under $300 on a group buy website, some direct-to-door site that keeps costs down that way. It's good enough that I miss it whenever I stay at someone else's house, though when I get a king/cali king I'm going to switch to latex because I love my solid latex pillow.

TL;DR: Don't skimp on things you'll be in contact with for over 2+ hours at a time or you'll regret it. Learn the physics of personal comfort, both as it goes for your body (i.e. Figure out where your lumbar is and what good posture is and then you'll understand why you want lumbar support in seating) and as it goes for the material in contact with your body (if you wear synthetic materials other than nylon/rayon, you are probably a pleb). Yes it's a lot to learn, you learn as you go, not all at once. Wear good socks and shoes and a breathable base layer with a comfortable mid layer that you can remove/add when going into warmer buildings (DOWN VESTS ARE FUCKING AWESOME).
